claim: MSI1 is expressed in stem and progenitor cells of neural and epithelial lineage.
source: The RNA-binding protein Musashi-1 (MSI1) is expressed in stem and progenitor cells of neural and epithelial lineage.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the central nervous system, MSI1 is expressed in astrocytes and committed glial and neural progenitor cells, but not in mature neurons and oligodendrocytes.
source: In the central nervous system, MSI1 is expressed in astrocytes and committed glial and neural progenitor cells, but not in mature neurons and oligodendrocytes (Figure 1A; Kaneko et al., 2000; Dobson et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies and reference to Figure 1A showing the expression pattern.

claim: MSI1 is routinely used as a marker for stem and progenitor cells in histological studies of neural and epithelial tissues.
source: In histological studies of neural and epithelial tissues, MSI1 is routinely used as a marker for stem and progenitor cells (Johnson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: MSI1 regulates neural development in mice and primary cells.
source: Analysis in mice and primary cells shows that MSI1 regulates neural development.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by subsequent detailed evidence from knockout mice studies.

claim: Msi1−/− knockout mice are uncoordinated, ataxic, develop hydrocephaly, and die within 1–2 months after birth.
source: Msi1−/− knockout mice are uncoordinated, ataxic, develop hydrocephaly, and die within 1–2 months after birth (Sakakibara et al., 2002).
evidence: This phenotype is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Msi1−/− knockout mouse brains are small, contain an expansion of early lineage progenitor cells, and display fewer mature cell types than normal.
source: Their brains are small, contain an expansion of early lineage progenitor cells, and display fewer mature cell types than normal (Sakakibara et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Embryonic neurospheres cultured from Msi1−/− mouse brains have a reduced capacity to differentiate into mature neurons and oligodendrocytes.
source: Embryonic neurospheres cultured from Msi1−/− mouse brains have a reduced capacity to differentiate into mature neurons and oligodendrocytes (Sakakibara et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: In primary oligodendrocyte progenitor cells, MSI1 promotes progenitor cell survival and prevents differentiation into mature oligodendrocytes.
source: In primary oligodendrocyte progenitor cells, MSI1 promotes progenitor cell survival and prevents differentiation into mature oligodendrocytes (Dobson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: MSI1 plays an early role in regulating neurogenesis and gliogenesis.
source: The phenotype and expression pattern reveal that MSI1 plays an early role in regulating neurogenesis and gliogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotype and expression pattern data described in the manuscript.

claim: MSI1 contains two RNA recognition Motifs (RRMs).
source: MSI1 contains two RNA recognition Motifs (RRMs) and is homologous to Drosophila melanogaster Musashi, a post-transcriptional regulatory protein that guides external sensory bristle patterning in flies (Sakakibara et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citation.

claim: MSI1 is homologous to Drosophila melanogaster Musashi, a post-transcriptional regulatory protein that guides external sensory bristle patterning in flies.
source: MSI1 contains two RNA recognition Motifs (RRMs) and is homologous to Drosophila melanogaster Musashi, a post-transcriptional regulatory protein that guides external sensory bristle patterning in flies (Sakakibara et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: In vitro SELEX experiments identified a series of aptamer sequences that bind to MSI1.
source: In vitro SELEX experiments identified a series of aptamer sequences that bind to MSI1 (Imai et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: A consensus sequence (G/A)U1–3AGU was present in most but not all of the MSI1-binding aptamers.
source: Visual inspection identified a consensus sequence (G/A)U1–3AGU that was present in most but not all of the aptamers.
evidence: This is based on analysis of SELEX data from cited work.

claim: NUMB is a MSI1 target and a repressor of NOTCH signaling.
source: A number of MSI1 targets have been identified by co-immunoprecipitation, including NUMB, a repressor of NOTCH signaling.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Numb transcripts harbor MSI1 consensus elements in the 3′-UTR.
source: Numb transcripts harbor MSI1 consensus elements in the 3′-UTR (Imai et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: MSI1 interacts with the Numb 3′-UTR in vitro.
source: MSI1 interacts with the Numb 3′-UTR in vitro, and Numb mRNA co-immunoprecipitates with MSI1 in transiently transfected NIH 3T3 cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Numb mRNA co-immunoprecipitates with MSI1 in transiently transfected NIH 3T3 cells.
source: MSI1 interacts with the Numb 3′-UTR in vitro, and Numb mRNA co-immunoprecipitates with MSI1 in transiently transfected NIH 3T3 cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Overexpression of MSI1 in NIH 3T3 cells decreases NUMB protein levels without affecting Numb mRNA.
source: Overexpression of MSI1 in NIH 3T3 cells decreases NUMB protein levels without affecting Numb mRNA and reduces the expression of a luciferase reporter in a 3′-UTR dependent manner (Imai et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: MSI1 negatively regulates Numb mRNA translation.
source: Together, the results show that MSI1 negatively regulates Numb mRNA translation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results described and cited.

claim: MSI1 acts as a translational activator in Xenopus laevis oocytes.
source: In contrast, MSI1 acts as a translational activator in Xenopus laevis oocytes, where it modulates cell cycle progression by regulating mRNA encoding the proto-oncogene Mos (Charlesworth et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: MSI1 promotes proliferation of numerous cancers of the brain and epithelial tissues.
source: MSI1 also promotes proliferation of numerous cancers of the brain and epithelial tissues (Toda et al., 2001; Hemmati et al., 2003; Yokota et al., 2004; Sanchez-Diaz et al., 2008; Sureban et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: MSI1 depletion in medulloblastoma and colorectal tumors results in decreased proliferation and increased apoptosis.
source: MSI1 depletion in medulloblastoma and colorectal tumors results in decreased proliferation and increased apoptosis (Sanchez-Diaz et al., 2008; Sureban et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: In colorectal tumors, MSI1 depletion is accompanied by inhibition of Notch-1 and upregulation of p21WAF1.
source: In colorectal tumors, MSI1 depletion is accompanied by inhibition of Notch-1 and upregulation of p21WAF1, a MSI1 target involved in cell cycle regulation (Battelli et al., 2006; Sureban et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Musashi-2 (MSI2) is 69% identical to MSI1 protein.
source: Musashi-2 (MSI2) is 69% identical to MSI1 protein and is expressed in a partially overlapping set of tissues (Sakakibara et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: MSI2 is expressed in a partially overlapping set of tissues compared to MSI1.
source: Musashi-2 (MSI2) is 69% identical to MSI1 protein and is expressed in a partially overlapping set of tissues (Sakakibara et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: MSI2 regulates hematopoesis and is involved in acute myeloid leukemia.
source: MSI2 regulates hematopoesis and is involved in acute myeloid leukemia (Ito et al., 2010; Kharas et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: In myeloid leukemia cells, MSI2 is highly expressed, and depletion results in decreased proliferation and increased apoptosis.
source: In myeloid leukemia cells, MSI2 is highly expressed, and depletion results in decreased proliferation and increased apoptosis (Kharas et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: The crisis phase of myeloid leukemia is marked by low NUMB expression.
source: The crisis phase of myeloid leukemia is marked by low NUMB expression (Ito et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Loss of MSI2 restores NUMB expression and impairs the blast crisis phase of myeloid leukemia.
source: Loss of MSI2 restores NUMB expression and impairs the blast crisis phase of myeloid leukemia (Ito et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: MSI2 expression levels are directly correlated with poor prognosis in myeloid leukemia patients.
source: Ultimately, MSI2 expression levels are directly correlated with poor prognosis in myeloid leukemia patients (Kharas et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: MSI1 binds with high affinity to the CCCR005 aptamer fragment.
source: MSI1 binds with high affinity to the aptamer fragment, which contains two copies of the consensus sequence.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the FP and F-EMSA data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The CCCR005 aptamer fragment contains two copies of the MSI1 consensus sequence.
source: MSI1 binds with high affinity to the aptamer fragment, which contains two copies of the consensus sequence.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: Four candidate inhibitors of MSI1 RNA-binding activity were identified from the small molecule screen.
source: Four candidate inhibitors were identified.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by the screening data in Table 1A.

claim: Chembridge compound 7409829 inhibits MSI1 with Ki, app, FP = 15 ± 2.8 µM and Ki, app, F–EMSA = 54 ± 22 µM.
source: The weakest inhibitor was the Chembridge compound 7409829 (Ki, app, FP = 15 ± 2.8 µM, Ki, app, F–EMSA = 54 ± 22 µM).
evidence: This is supported by dose response experimental data.

claim: Aurintricarboxylic acid (ATA) inhibits MSI1 with Ki, app, FP = 230 ± 30 nM and Ki, app, F–EMSA = 1.55 ± 0.14 µM.
source: The most potent inhibitor was aurintricarboxylic acid (ATA, Ki, app, FP = 230 ± 30 nM, Ki, app, F–EMSA = 1.55 ± 0.14 µM), a compound that readily polymerizes in aqueous solution to form a polyanion.
evidence: This is supported by dose response experimental data.

claim: Aurintricarboxylic acid readily polymerizes in aqueous solution to form a polyanion.
source: The most potent inhibitor was aurintricarboxylic acid (ATA, Ki, app, FP = 230 ± 30 nM, Ki, app, F–EMSA = 1.55 ± 0.14 µM), a compound that readily polymerizes in aqueous solution to form a polyanion.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about ATA.

claim: Aurintricarboxylic acid has been identified in many high throughput small molecule assays as a non-specific inhibitor of protein–nucleic acid interactions.
source: This compound has been identified in many high throughput small molecule assays as a non-specific inhibitor of protein–nucleic acid interactions (Lam et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: GW7647 is a PPARα agonist.
source: The next inhibitor was GW7647, a PPARα agonist (Berger and Moller, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: GW7647 inhibits MSI1 with Ki, app = 6.5 ± 0.4 µM by FP and 21 ± 0.8 µM by F–EMSA.
source: The Ki, app for this compound was 6.5 ± 0.4 µM by FP and 21 ± 0.8 µM by F–EMSA.
evidence: This is supported by dose response experimental data.

claim: PPARα is a nuclear hormone receptor that is activated by long chain unsaturated fatty acids.
source: PPARα is a nuclear hormone receptor that is activated by long chain unsaturated fatty acids (Gottlicher et al., 1992; Bocos et al., 1995; Forman et al., 1997; Kliewer et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Oleic acid is an eighteen-carbon monounsaturated fatty acid with one double bond located nine carbons from the aliphatic—omega—end of the molecule (18:1, ω-9).
source: The final inhibitor was oleic acid, an eighteen-carbon monounsaturated fatty acid with one double bond located nine carbons from the aliphatic—omega—end of the molecule (18:1, ω-9).
evidence: This is based on established chemical knowledge.

claim: Oleic acid inhibits MSI1 with apparent Ki of 1.2 ± 0.4 µM by FP and 1.4 ± 0.7 µM by F–EMSA.
source: The apparent Ki of this compound was 1.2 ± 0.4 µM by FP and 1.4 ± 0.7 µM by F–EMSA, and we observed decreased affinity for the RNA aptamer with increasing concentrations of oleic acid (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by dose response experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The Ki, app of oleic acid is approximately two orders of magnitude below the critical micelle concentration (CMC) in the equilibration buffer (pH 8.0).
source: The Ki, app is approximately two orders of magnitude below the critical micelle concentration (CMC) in our equilibration buffer (pH 8.0) as measured by N-phenyl-1-naphthylamine (CMC ≥ 75 ± 8 µM, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by CMC determination experiments shown in the figure.

claim: Oleic acid has been screened in 754 bioassays reported in the PubChem database.
source: Oleic acid has been screened in 754 bioassays reported in the PubChem database.
evidence: This is based on data from the PubChem database.

claim: Oleic acid scored as positive in 4% of the bioassays in the PubChem database.
source: Of these, oleic acid scored as positive in 4% of the assays.
evidence: This is based on analysis of PubChem database data.

claim: Only 14 unique proteins are responsive to oleic acid in PubChem bioassays.
source: In total, only 14 unique proteins are responsive to oleic acid.
evidence: This is based on analysis of PubChem database data.

claim: Oleic acid inhibition of MSI1 is specific.
source: This suggests that oleic acid inhibition is specific.
evidence: This is inferred from the low hit rate in PubChem bioassays.

claim: Oleic acid is the most abundant fatty acid in body fat.
source: Oleic acid is the most abundant fatty acid in body fat and is produced by mature oligodendrocytes during myelination (Martinez and Mougan, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Oleic acid is produced by mature oligodendrocytes during myelination.
source: Oleic acid is the most abundant fatty acid in body fat and is produced by mature oligodendrocytes during myelination (Martinez and Mougan, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Eicosenoic acid (20:1, ω-9) inhibits MSI1 with a potency similar to oleic acid (Ki, app, FP = 1.2 ± 0.4 µM, Ki, app, F–EMSA = 1.7 ± 0.6 µM).
source: Eicosenoic acid (20:1, ω-9) inhibited MSI1 with a potency similar to oleic acid (Ki, app, FP = 1.2 ± 0.4 µM, Ki, app, F–EMSA = 1.7 ± 0.6 µM).
evidence: This is supported by dose response experimental data.

claim: Erucic acid (22:1, ω-9) is a stronger inhibitor of MSI1 than oleic acid (Ki, app, FP = 640 ± 150 nM, Ki, app, F–EMSA = 820 ± 30 nM).
source: Erucic acid (22:1, ω-9) was a stronger inhibitor (Ki, app, FP = 640 ± 150 nM, Ki, app, F–EMSA = 820 ± 30 nM), and nervonic acid (24:1, ω-9) inhibited more weakly (Ki, app, FP = 47 ± 25 µM, Ki, app, F–EMSA = 23 ± 8 µM).
evidence: This is supported by dose response experimental data.

claim: Nervonic acid (24:1, ω-9) inhibits MSI1 more weakly than oleic acid (Ki, app, FP = 47 ± 25 µM, Ki, app, F–EMSA = 23 ± 8 µM).
source: Erucic acid (22:1, ω-9) was a stronger inhibitor (Ki, app, FP = 640 ± 150 nM, Ki, app, F–EMSA = 820 ± 30 nM), and nervonic acid (24:1, ω-9) inhibited more weakly (Ki, app, FP = 47 ± 25 µM, Ki, app, F–EMSA = 23 ± 8 µM).
evidence: This is supported by dose response experimental data.

claim: Palmitoleic acid (16:1, ω-7) has a moderate effect on MSI1 inhibition (Ki, app, FP = 5.3 ± 0.5 µM, Ki, app, F–EMSA = 12 ± 0.9 µM).
source: Removing two carbons (palmitoleic acid, 16:1, ω-7) had a moderate effect on inhibition (Ki, app, FP = 5.3 ± 0.5 µM, Ki, app, F–EMSA = 12 ± 0.9 µM).
evidence: This is supported by dose response experimental data.

claim: Ricinoleic acid (12-hydroxy-oleic acid) has reduced inhibitory effect on MSI1 compared to oleic acid (Ki, app, F–EMSA = 18 ± 9).
source: The presence of a hydroxyl group at carbon 12 (ricinoleic acid, 12-hydroxy-oleic acid) had a stronger effect; inhibition is barely detectable by FP and reduced 15-fold in F–EMSA measurements (Ki, app, F–EMSA = 18 ± 9).
evidence: This is supported by dose response experimental data.

claim: Oleamide, ethyl oleate, and 4-methylumbelliferyl oleate failed to inhibit MSI1 RNA-binding.
source: Oleamide, ethyl oleate, and 4-methylumbelliferyl oleate failed to inhibit RNA-binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental testing of these compounds.

claim: The presence of a Coenzyme A (CoA) substituent on oleic acid is apparently tolerated for MSI1 inhibition.
source: In contrast, the presence of a Coenzyme A (CoA) substituent was apparently tolerated, although we noted some deacylation of acyl-CoA stocks by thin layer chromatography.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Stearic (18:0), palmitic (16:0), and myristic (14:0) acids failed to inhibit MSI1 RNA-binding activity.
source: Stearic (18:0), palmitic (16:0), and myristic (14:0) acids failed to inhibit MSI1 RNA-binding activity, indicating that the ω-9 double bond is required.
evidence: This is supported by experimental testing of these compounds.

claim: The ω-9 double bond is required for MSI1 inhibition by fatty acids.
source: Stearic (18:0), palmitic (16:0), and myristic (14:0) acids failed to inhibit MSI1 RNA-binding activity, indicating that the ω-9 double bond is required.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing saturated fatty acids do not inhibit MSI1.

claim: The orientation of the ω-9 double bond is critical for MSI1 inhibition.
source: Surprisingly, the orientation of the double bond is also critical.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing elaidic acid does not inhibit MSI1.

claim: Elaidic acid (18:1, ω-9 trans) did not inhibit MSI1.
source: Elaidic acid (18:1, ω-9 trans) has the same molecular weight as oleic acid, and nearly identical refractive index and molar aqueous solubility (∼10 mM at pH 8.0), but its ω-9 double bond is trans rather than cis. Elaidic acid did not inhibit MSI1 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Linoleic acid (18:2, ω-9, ω-6) inhibits MSI1 with Ki, app, FP = 2.2 ± 0.2 µM and Ki, app, F–EMSA = 1.2 ± 0.03 µM.
source: Linoleic (18:2, ω-9, ω-6) and arachidonic (20:4, ω-12, ω-9, ω-6, ω-3) polyunsaturated fatty acids also inhibit MSI1, but with a weaker apparent inhibition constant (Linoleic acid: Ki, app, FP = 2.2 ± 0.2 µM, Ki, app, F–EMSA = 1.2 ± 0.03 µM; Arachidonic acid: Ki, app, FP = 3.0 ± 0.2 µM, Ki, app, F–EMSA = 1.1 ± 0.3 µM).
evidence: This is supported by dose response experimental data.

claim: Arachidonic acid (20:4, ω-12, ω-9, ω-6, ω-3) inhibits MSI1 with Ki, app, FP = 3.0 ± 0.2 µM and Ki, app, F–EMSA = 1.1 ± 0.3 µM.
source: Linoleic (18:2, ω-9, ω-6) and arachidonic (20:4, ω-12, ω-9, ω-6, ω-3) polyunsaturated fatty acids also inhibit MSI1, but with a weaker apparent inhibition constant (Linoleic acid: Ki, app, FP = 2.2 ± 0.2 µM, Ki, app, F–EMSA = 1.2 ± 0.03 µM; Arachidonic acid: Ki, app, FP = 3.0 ± 0.2 µM, Ki, app, F–EMSA = 1.1 ± 0.3 µM).
evidence: This is supported by dose response experimental data.

claim: Omega-9 cis unsaturated fatty acids between 18 and 22 carbons specifically inhibit MSI1 RNA-binding activity.
source: We conclude that omega-9 cis unsaturated fatty acids between 18 and 22 carbons specifically inhibit MSI1 RNA-binding activity and identify erucic acid as the most potent inhibitor (Table 1).
evidence: This is concluded from the structure-activity relationship data.

claim: Erucic acid is the most potent inhibitor of MSI1 among the fatty acids tested.
source: We conclude that omega-9 cis unsaturated fatty acids between 18 and 22 carbons specifically inhibit MSI1 RNA-binding activity and identify erucic acid as the most potent inhibitor (Table 1).
evidence: This is concluded from the dose response data.

claim: MSI2 was inhibited by fatty acids with similar specificity to MSI1.
source: MSI2 was inhibited with similar specificity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Titration of oleic acid, but not elaidic acid, strongly quenched MSI1 tryptophan fluorescence.
source: Titration of oleic acid, but not elaidic acid, strongly quenched tryptophan fluorescence and altered the emission intensity curve shape from 300 to 400 nm (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Neither oleic acid nor elaidic acid affected the fluorescence of NATA.
source: Neither compound affected the fluorescence of NATA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The Kd, app of oleic acid for MSI1 is 2.6 ± 1 µM as measured by tryptophan fluorescence.
source: The Kd, app of oleic acid was 2.6 ± 1 µM, essentially identical to the Ki, app determined by FP and F–EMSA dose response experiments (Table 1A; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by tryptophan fluorescence experimental data.

claim: Oleic acid inhibition results from a direct association of oleic acid with the MSI1 protein.
source: Our data are consistent with inhibition resulting from a direct association of oleic acid with the MSI1 protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the tryptophan fluorescence data.

claim: A hydrophobic cavity exists on the alpha-helical surface of MSI1 RRM1, opposite the RNA-binding surface.
source: After examining the published NMR structures, we were intrigued to note a hydrophobic cavity on the alpha-helical surface of RRM1, opposite the RNA-binding surface (Figure 2B) and adjacent to W29 (Nagata et al., 1999; Miyanoiri et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published NMR structures.

claim: MSI1 RRM2 does not have a hydrophobic cavity like RRM1.
source: MSI1 RRM2 does not have this feature.
evidence: This is based on analysis of published NMR structures.

claim: MSI1 RRM1 (amino acids 7-103) bound to the aptamer RNA with an apparent Kd of 75.2 ± 10 nM by FP.
source: RRM1 bound to the aptamer RNA with an apparent Kd of 75.2 ± 10 nM by FP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by FP experimental data.

claim: Addition of oleic acid but not elaidic acid inhibits MSI1 RRM1 RNA-binding activity with similar Ki, app compared to the full RNA-binding domain.
source: Addition of oleic acid but not elaidic acid inhibits RNA-binding activity with similar Ki, app compared to the full RNA-binding domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: RRM1 is sufficient for RNA recognition and fatty acid inhibition.
source: Thus, RRM1 is sufficient for RNA recognition and fatty acid inhibition.
evidence: This is concluded from the RRM1 binding and inhibition experiments.

claim: The addition of increasing amounts of oleic acid to MSI1 resulted in considerable reduction of NMR peak intensities and line broadening.
source: The addition of increasing amounts of oleic acid did not result in significant changes in chemical shifts but in considerable reduction of the peak intensities and in line broadening.
evidence: This is based on NMR experimental observations.

claim: The largest loss of NMR signal upon addition of substoichiometric concentrations of oleic acid was observed for W29, Q30, L36, C49, L50, R53, S60, G62, V74, T89, and K98.
source: The largest loss of signal upon addition of substoichiometric concentrations of oleic acid was observed for W29, Q30, L36, C49, L50, R53, S60, G62, V74, T89, and K98 (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2E,F).
evidence: This is based on NMR experimental data.

claim: The observed loss of NMR signal is likely due to chemical exchange between the free and bound state of MSI1.
source: The observed loss of signal is likely due to chemical exchange between the free and bound state.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR data.

claim: Oleic acid binding alters the secondary structure of MSI1.
source: We conclude that oleic acid binding alters the secondary structure of MSI1, but this transition does not appear to induce aggregation at concentrations below the CMC.
evidence: This is concluded from CD and AUC experimental data.

claim: Oleic acid binding does not appear to induce MSI1 aggregation at concentrations below the CMC.
source: We conclude that oleic acid binding alters the secondary structure of MSI1, but this transition does not appear to induce aggregation at concentrations below the CMC.
evidence: This is concluded from AUC experimental data.

claim: In the docked models, both eicosenoic acid and oleic acid insert the ω-9 end into the hydrophobic cavity of MSI1 RRM1.
source: In the docked models, both compounds insert the ω-9 end into the cavity, form extensive contacts with the protein surface, and position their carboxy termini adjacent to a positively charged arginine side chain (R53 or R61, dependent on the model, Figure 3A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on computational docking calculations.

claim: In the docked models, fatty acids position their carboxy termini adjacent to R53 or R61.
source: In the docked models, both compounds insert the ω-9 end into the cavity, form extensive contacts with the protein surface, and position their carboxy termini adjacent to a positively charged arginine side chain (R53 or R61, dependent on the model, Figure 3A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on computational docking calculations.

claim: Upon oleic acid binding, MSI1 underwent a transition to a more open state characterized by an increase in solvent accessible surface area (SASA) and radius of gyration.
source: Upon oleic acid binding, MSI1 underwent a transition to a more open state characterized by an increase in solvent accessible surface area (SASA) and radius of gyration (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Binding of oleic acid is associated with stabilization of the C-terminus of α-helix 1 in MSI1 RRM1.
source: Direct visualization of the structure's time evolution showed that binding of oleic acid is associated with stabilization of the C-terminus of α-helix 1, fraying of α-helix 2 at both the N- and C-termini and, in one trajectory, formation of an additional β-sheet in loop 5 (Figure 3C,D; Video 1).
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Binding of oleic acid is associated with fraying of α-helix 2 at both the N- and C-termini in MSI1 RRM1.
source: Direct visualization of the structure's time evolution showed that binding of oleic acid is associated with stabilization of the C-terminus of α-helix 1, fraying of α-helix 2 at both the N- and C-termini and, in one trajectory, formation of an additional β-sheet in loop 5 (Figure 3C,D; Video 1).
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: In one MD trajectory, binding of oleic acid is associated with formation of an additional β-sheet in loop 5 of MSI1 RRM1.
source: Direct visualization of the structure's time evolution showed that binding of oleic acid is associated with stabilization of the C-terminus of α-helix 1, fraying of α-helix 2 at both the N- and C-termini and, in one trajectory, formation of an additional β-sheet in loop 5 (Figure 3C,D; Video 1).
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The β-sheet that forms in loop 5 upon oleic acid binding is absent in the MSI1 apo structure but is present in the structure of MSI1 bound to RNA.
source: Notably, the β-sheet that forms in loop 5 is absent in the MSI1 apo structure but is present in the structure of MSI1 bound to RNA (Figure 3D; Ohyama et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on comparison of MD simulation data with published NMR structures.

claim: The circular dichroism and analytical ultracentrifugation data are consistent with a net gain in secondary structure upon oleic acid binding.
source: The circular dichroism and analytical ultracentrifugation data (Figure 2C,D, Figure 2—figure supplement1E) are consistent with a net gain in secondary structure upon oleic acid binding, as predicted by the MD simulation (Figure 3, Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data with MD simulation predictions.

claim: The change in tryptophan fluorescence observed upon oleic acid but not elaidic acid treatment is consistent with the changes in tryptophan solvent exposure observed in the MD simulation.
source: In addition, the change in tryptophan fluorescence observed upon oleic acid but not elaidic acid treatment is consistent with the changes in tryptophan solvent exposure observed in the simulation.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data with MD simulation predictions.

claim: Mutation of Q30 to glutamate had no effect on fatty acid inhibition of MSI1 (Krel, app = 0.9).
source: We observed no change in fatty acid inhibition when Q30 was mutated to a glutamate (Krel, app = 0.9, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis and FP experimental data.

claim: Mutation of H83 to leucine had no effect on fatty acid inhibition of MSI1.
source: Mutation of H83 to leucine also had no effect on fatty acid inhibition.
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis and FP experimental data.

claim: Mutation of H83 to phenylalanine reduced MSI1 inhibition by fatty acids by almost twofold.
source: Mutation of H83 to phenylalanine reduced inhibition by almost twofold.
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis and FP experimental data.

claim: Mutation of G64 to alanine reduced MSI1 inhibition by fatty acids by 3.1-fold.
source: Mutation of G64 to alanine reduced inhibition by 3.1-fold.
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis and FP experimental data.

claim: Mutation of G35 to aspartate results in a twofold reduction of MSI1 inhibition by fatty acids.
source: Mutation of G35 to aspartate and glutamate results in a twofold and sevenfold reduction of inhibition, respectively.
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis and FP experimental data.

claim: Mutation of G35 to glutamate results in a sevenfold reduction of MSI1 inhibition by fatty acids.
source: Mutation of G35 to aspartate and glutamate results in a twofold and sevenfold reduction of inhibition, respectively.
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis and FP experimental data.

claim: Oleic acid inhibition of the MSI1 R53E mutant is reduced threefold.
source: Oleic acid inhibition of the R53E mutant is reduced threefold, while R61E is reduced fivefold.
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis and FP experimental data.

claim: Oleic acid inhibition of the MSI1 R61E mutant is reduced fivefold.
source: Oleic acid inhibition of the R53E mutant is reduced threefold, while R61E is reduced fivefold.
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis and FP experimental data.

claim: Mutating both R53 and R61 to glutamate (R53E/R61E) increases the reduction of MSI1 inhibition by fatty acids to 35-fold.
source: Mutating both arginines (R53E/R61E) increases this effect to 35-fold.
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis and FP experimental data.

claim: R53 and R61 are both important for MSI1 inhibition by fatty acids, and act in a partially redundant way.
source: This indicates that R53 and R61 are both important for inhibition, and act in a partially redundant way.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data.

claim: The R53E mutant has a small effect on MSI1 RNA-binding.
source: The R53E mutant has a small effect on RNA-binding, while the R61E mutant has a strong 18-fold effect.
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis and binding experimental data.

claim: The R61E mutant has a strong 18-fold effect on MSI1 RNA-binding.
source: The R53E mutant has a small effect on RNA-binding, while the R61E mutant has a strong 18-fold effect.
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis and binding experimental data.

claim: The MD simulations and experimental data are consistent with an allosteric model of inhibition, wherein fatty acid binding induces a change in conformation that modifies the secondary structure of RRM1 and perturbs the position of amino acids required for RNA recognition.
source: Together, the MD simulations and experimental data are consistent with an allosteric model of inhibition, wherein fatty acid binding induces a change in conformation that modifies the secondary structure of RRM1 and perturbs the position of amino acids required for RNA recognition.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined computational and experimental data.

claim: CG-4 cells maintain normal precursor cell morphology, can be readily transfected, and can be induced to differentiate into mature oligodendrocytes by withdrawal of growth factors.
source: CG-4 cells maintain normal precursor cell morphology, can be readily transfected, and can be induced to differentiate into mature oligodendrocytes by withdrawal of growth factors (Louis et al., 1992; Franklin et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Mature oligodendrocytes produce myelin, a lipid-rich membrane structure that insulates neuronal axons.
source: Mature oligodendrocytes produce myelin, a lipid-rich membrane structure that insulates neuronal axons to both protect them and to aid in saltatory impulse conductance throughout the CNS (Griffiths et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work and represents established knowledge.

claim: The lipid and fatty acid profiles of mature oligodendrocyte-rich white matter differ from that of the grey matter.
source: The lipid and fatty acid profiles of mature oligodendrocyte-rich white matter differ from that of the grey matter (Figure 5–figure supplement 3, Martinez and Mougan, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work and data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: CG-4 cells shift lipid profiles upon differentiation.
source: CG-4 cells also shift lipid profiles upon differentiation, as detected by quantitative lipidomics mass spectrometry (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: MSI1 is expressed strongly in CG-4 progenitor cells but decreases upon differentiation (OPCs: 1.0 ± 0.3, oligodendrocytes: 0.15 ± 0.01, p-value=0.0035).
source: As with primary OPCs, MSI1 is expressed strongly in the precursor state but decreases upon differentiation (OPCs: 1.0 ± 0.3, oligodendrocytes: 0.15 ± 0.01, p-value=0.0035).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: Treatment of CG-4 OPCs with oleic acid strongly inhibited the rate of cell proliferation.
source: Treatment of CG-4 OPCs with oleic acid strongly inhibited the rate of cell proliferation (Figure 5), matching the published phenotype of MSI1 knock down in primary OPCs (Dobson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Treating HEK293T cells with oleic acid had little or no effect on the rate of proliferation.
source: In contrast, treating HEK293T cells—which do not express MSI1—with the same concentration of oleic acid had little or no effect on the rate of proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation assay data.

claim: Treatment with stearic acid had no effect on proliferation rate in either CG-4 or HEK293T cells.
source: Treatment with stearic acid, which does not inhibit MSI1, had no effect on proliferation rate in either cell type (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Reduction of MSI1 activity by oleic acid limits proliferation of CG-4 cells.
source: The data suggest that reduction of MSI1 activity by oleic acid limits proliferation, but we cannot rule out that the fatty acid modulates other cellular pathways that contribute to proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell proliferation data, though alternative explanations are acknowledged.

claim: There are seven MSI1 consensus sites in the 3′-UTR of Scd-1 mRNA.
source: There are seven MSI1 consensus sites in the 3′-UTR of Scd-1 mRNA.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of the Scd-1 3′-UTR.

claim: MSI1 binds to all seven putative consensus sites in the Scd1 3′-UTR by FP and F–EMSA.
source: MSI1 binds to all seven sites by FP and F–EMSA (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Site 2 and site 7 of the Scd1 3′-UTR bind to MSI1 with comparable affinity to the selected aptamer.
source: Site 2 and site 7 bind to MSI1 with comparable affinity to the selected aptamer.
evidence: This is based on binding affinity measurements.

claim: Transcripts encoding SCD1 co-immunoprecipitated with MSI1 from CG-4 cell extracts using two independent antibodies.
source: Transcripts encoding SCD1 co-immunopreciptated with MSI1 from CG-4 cell extracts using two independent antibodies (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experimental data.

claim: Overexpression of MSI1 in HEK293T cells increased the amount of SCD and SCD proteolysis products by 2.5 ± 0.35-fold (p-value=0.018).
source: Overexpression of MSI1 in HEK293T cells, which do not endogenously express MSI1, increased the amount of SCD and SCD proteolysis products by 2.5 ± 0.35-fold (p-value=0.018, Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot experimental data.

claim: qRT-PCR analysis of HEK293T mRNA shows a slight but non-significant increase in SCD1 transcript abundance upon MSI1 overexpression.
source: qRT-PCR analysis of HEK293T mRNA shows a slight but non-significant increase in SCD1 transcript abundance upon MSI1 overexpression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR experimental data.

claim: Statistically significant changes ranging from 2- to 32-fold were observed in 54 of the 312 lipids assayed in HEK293T cells with MSI1 expression (FDR = 0.05).
source: We observed statistically significant changes ranging from 2- to 32-fold in 54 of the 312 lipids assayed (FDR = 0.05, Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics mass spectrometry data.

claim: 50 of 54 significant lipid changes in HEK293T cells with MSI1 expression were positive, indicating that MSI1 expression stimulates production of certain lipids.
source: We noted positive changes in 50 of 54 significant data points, indicating that MSI1 expression stimulates production of certain lipids.
evidence: This is based on analysis of lipidomics data.

claim: 38 of the significantly changing lipids in HEK293T cells with MSI1 expression fell into one of three cholesterol and triacylgylcerol (TAG) classes: cholesterol esters, 16:0 acyl-containing TAG, and 16:1 acyl-containing TAG.
source: 38 of the significantly changing lipids fell into one of three cholesterol and triacylgylcerol (TAG) classes: cholesterol esters, 16:0 acyl-containing TAG, and 16:1 acyl-containing TAG (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: This is based on analysis of lipidomics data.

claim: Cholesterol esters and TAGs are made using SCD products.
source: Cholesterol esters and TAGs are made using SCD products, and have been shown to be more abundant in mice overexpressing SCD1, and less abundant in liver SCD1 knockout mice (Miyazaki et al., 2000; Attie et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: SCD activity is upregulated in the presence of MSI1 in HEK293T cells.
source: This indicates that SCD activity is upregulated in the presence of MSI1.
evidence: This is inferred from the lipidomics data showing increased cholesterol esters and TAGs.

claim: Stearoyl-CoA desaturase expression is increased in the presence of MSI1.
source: Together, our binding data, co-immunoprecipitation, western blots, and lipidomics profiling results show that stearoyl-CoA desaturase expression is increased in the presence of MSI1, possibly through direct association with consensus motifs in the 3′-UTR of SCD transcripts.
evidence: This is concluded from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Of 2107 annotated 3′ UTRs for genes involved with lipid, cholesterol, fatty acid biosynthesis, and SREBP activity, 1275 contain at least one MSI1 binding element.
source: We note that of 2107 annotated 3′ UTRs for genes involved with lipid, cholesterol, fatty acid biosynthesis, and SREBP activity, 1275 contain at least one MSI1 binding element.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of 3′ UTR sequences.

claim: A survey of 64 genes that associate with MSI1 in a RIP-ChIP experiment reveals that 8 are annotated to be involved with lipid metabolic processes.
source: Indeed, a survey of 64 genes that associate with MSI1 in a RIP-ChIP experiment reveals that 8 are annotated to be involved with lipid metabolic processes (de Sousa Abreu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published RIP-ChIP data.

claim: Long chain ω-9 fatty acids between 18 and 22 carbons in length are allosteric inhibitors of MSI1 RNA binding activity.
source: Our data reveal that the long chain ω-9 fatty acids oleic acids between 18 and 22 carbons in length are allosteric inhibitors of MSI1 RNA binding activity.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined experimental and computational data.

claim: SCD, the enzyme that catalyzes the ω-9 desaturation, is a MSI1 regulatory target.
source: Our data also show that SCD, the enzyme that catalyzes the ω-9 desaturation, is a MSI1 regulatory target.
evidence: This is concluded from the binding, co-IP, western blot, and lipidomics data.

claim: MSI1 controls cellular proliferation through a feedback loop that includes SCD and its enzymatic products, such as oleic acid.
source: The results are consistent with a model where MSI1 controls cellular proliferation through a feedback loop that includes SCD and its enzymatic products, such as oleic acid (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the combined experimental data.

claim: Oleic acid is the precursor for synthesis of longer chain fatty acids such as eicosanoic, erucic, and nervonic acid.
source: Oleic acid is the precursor for synthesis of longer chain fatty acids such as eicosanoic, erucic, and nervonic acid, signaling molecules such as arachidonic acid, endocannabinoids, and prostaglandins, and membrane phospholipids.
evidence: This is based on established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Oleic acid is abundant in the lipid-rich myelin membranes produced by mature oligodendrocytes.
source: Oleic acid is abundant in the lipid-rich myelin membranes produced by mature oligodendrocytes (Martinez and Mougan, 1998), and CG-4 OPCs show global changes in the lipid profile upon differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: OPCs express MSI1, but mature myelinating oligodendrocytes do not.
source: OPCs express MSI1, but mature myelinating oligodendrocytes do not (Dobson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: In the oligodendrocyte lineage, oleic acid and MSI1 levels are anti-correlated.
source: In the oligodendrocyte lineage, oleic acid, and MSI1 levels are anti-correlated, which suggests a possible biological role for MSI1 inhibition by fatty acids (Martinez and Mougan, 1998; Dobson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature on oleic acid and MSI1 expression patterns.

claim: PPARs are nuclear hormone receptor proteins that regulate cellular processes including fatty acid metabolism, differentiation, cell cycling, and inflammation.
source: PPARs are nuclear hormone receptor proteins that regulate cellular processes including fatty acid metabolism, differentiation, cell cycling, and inflammation (Berger and Moller, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work and represents established knowledge.

claim: PPARγ agonists accelerate oligodendrocyte maturation.
source: PPARγ agonists accelerate oligodendrocyte maturation (De Nuccio et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Both GW7647 and oleic acid function as PPAR agonists.
source: Both GW7647 and oleic acid function as PPAR agonists, and both inhibit MSI1 RNA-binding activity, suggesting that MSI1 and PPARs possibly regulate gene expression in a reciprocal fashion.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about these compounds.

claim: MSI1 and PPARs possibly regulate gene expression in a reciprocal fashion.
source: Both GW7647 and oleic acid function as PPAR agonists, and both inhibit MSI1 RNA-binding activity, suggesting that MSI1 and PPARs possibly regulate gene expression in a reciprocal fashion.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that both PPAR agonists inhibit MSI1.

claim: The two human isoforms of SCD, SCD1 and SCD5, catalyze the conversion of saturated fatty acids (SFAs) into monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs).
source: The two human isoforms of SCD, SCD1 and SCD5, catalyze the conversion of saturated fatty acids (SFAs) into monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) (Zhang et al., 1999; Beiraghi et al., 2003; Minville-Walz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work and represents established knowledge.

claim: MUFAs are used in the synthesis of numerous lipids, including phospholipids, di- and triacylglycerols, cholesterol esters, and signaling molecules such as eicosanoids.
source: MUFAs are then used in the synthesis of numerous lipids, including phospholipids, di- and triacylglycerols, cholesterol esters, and signaling molecules such as eicosanoids.
evidence: This is based on established biochemical knowledge.

claim: SCD is an essential enzyme to normal cellular proliferation, metabolism, and signaling.
source: SCD is therefore an essential enzyme to normal cellular proliferation, metabolism, and signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the role of SCD in lipid synthesis.

claim: The Penalva group identified 64 putative MSI1 targets using a RIP-ChIP analysis in HEK293T cells.
source: The Penalva group identified 64 putative MSI1 targets using a RIP-ChIP analysis in HEK293T cells (de Sousa Abreu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Of 64 putative MSI1 targets identified by RIP-ChIP, eight are annotated to play a role in lipid, fatty acid, or cholesterol metabolic processes.
source: Of these putative targets, eight are annotated to play a role in lipid, fatty acid, or cholesterol metabolic processes.
evidence: This is based on analysis of published RIP-ChIP data.

claim: SCD has been implicated in a number of disease states, including obesity, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and cancer.
source: SCD has been implicated in a number of disease states, including obesity, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and cancer.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Obese and diabetic animals produce abnormally high levels of TAGs and cholesterol esters.
source: Obese and diabetic animals produce abnormally high levels of TAGs and cholesterol esters (Coleman and Lee, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: TAGs and cholesterol esters are elevated in a hyperlipidemia mouse model that overexpresses SCD.
source: These energy storage molecules are also elevated in a hyperlipidemia mouse model that overexpresses SCD (Attie et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: SCD1 knockout mice display impaired biosythesis of both TAGs and cholesterol esters.
source: Conversely, SCD1 knockout mice display impaired biosythesis of both TAGs and cholesterol esters (Miyazaki et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: SCD is upregulated in tumor cells, including colonic and esophageal carcinoma.
source: SCD is upregulated in tumor cells, including colonic and esophageal carcinoma (Li et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Cancerous cells use newly synthesized lipids primarily for phospholipid production, which are used in new membranes.
source: Cancerous cells use newly synthesized lipids primarily for phospholipid production, which are used in new membranes (Swinnen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: SCD1 activates the oncogenic Akt and AMPK signaling pathways.
source: Additionally, new evidence suggests that SCD1 activates the oncogenic Akt and AMPK signaling pathways (Scaglia and Igal, 2008; Scaglia et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: SCD regulates SFA and MUFA homeostasis.
source: SCD regulates SFA and MUFA homeostasis, and therefore plays an integral role in lipid signaling pathways.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about SCD function.

claim: SFAs serve as proinflammatory factors by acting as ligands for immune receptors such as those in the Toll-like receptor family.
source: SFAs serve as proinflammatory factors by acting as ligands for immune receptors such as those in the Toll-like receptor family (Shi et al., 2006; Nguyen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: MUFA products of SCD are further modified to become polyunsaturated fatty acids, such as arachidonic acid, which are converted into eicosanoids by cyclooxygenases.
source: MUFA products of SCD are further modified to become polyunsaturated fatty acids, such as arachidonic acid, which are converted into eicosanoids by cyclooxygenases (James et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work and represents established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Eicosanoids serve as proinflammatory and immune signaling molecules.
source: Eicosanoids serve as proinflammatory and immune signaling molecules (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work and represents established knowledge.

claim: SCD is linked to Wnt signaling through mediation of the palmitic/palmitoleic acid conversion, as active Wnt proteins require conjugation of palmitoleic acid.
source: Recent data also link SCD to Wnt signaling through mediation of the palmitic/palmitoleic acid conversion, as active Wnt proteins require conjugation of palmitoleic acid (Rios-Esteves and Resh, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: The balance between SFAs and MUFAs must be tightly controlled.
source: The balance between SFAs and MUFAs must be tightly controlled, and while SCD is not the only enzyme involved in the process, it does serve as an essential gatekeeper in the conversion of dietary SFA to MUFA.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about lipid metabolism.

claim: Fatty acids associate with membrane-bound sterol responsive element binding protein (SREBP) to inhibit a cleavage event that produces the activated form of SREBP.
source: For example, fatty acids associate with membrane-bound sterol responsive element binding protein (SREBP) to inhibit a cleavage event that produces the activated form of SREBP, a transcription factor involved in lipid homeostasis (Wang et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Free fatty acids stimulate proinflammatory cytokine expression while decreasing anti-inflammatory cytokine expression in adipocytes.
source: Free fatty acids have been shown to stimulate proinflammatory cytokine expression while decreasing anti-inflammatory cytokine expression in adipocytes (Bradley et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Treatment of various tumor lines with oleic acid results in transcriptional inhibition of the Her-2/neu (erbB-2) oncogene through PEA3.
source: Interestingly, treatment of various tumor lines with oleic acid results in transcriptional inhibition of the Her-2/neu (erbB-2) oncogene through PEA3, although the precise mechanism of regulation remains unknown (Menendez et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: In yeast cells, fatty acids bind oleate-activated transcription factors (OAFs) to effect transcription of genes responsible for fatty acid metabolism, glucose metabolism, stress response, and other related processes.
source: In yeast cells, fatty acids bind oleate-activated transcription factors (OAFs) to effect transcription of genes responsible for fatty acid metabolism, glucose metabolism, stress response, and other related processes (Gurvitz and Rottensteiner, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: MSI1 is the first example of a fatty acid-responsive RNA binding protein.
source: Although numerous transcription factors are regulated by fatty acids, to our knowledge, MSI1 is the first example of a fatty acid-responsive RNA binding protein.
evidence: This is claimed based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Integration of metabolite sensing and post-transcriptional regulation is widespread in bacteria.
source: Integration of metabolite sensing and post-transcriptional regulation is widespread in bacteria, but relatively few examples have been found in eukaryotes (Winkler and Breaker, 2003; Roth and Breaker, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Riboswitches regulate gene expression at the RNA level in response to intermediary metabolites.
source: Riboswitches regulate gene expression at the RNA level in response to intermediary metabolites.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about riboswitches.

claim: Small molecule metabolites bind mRNA transcripts, usually in the 5′ UTR, to induce a structural change that interferes with the transcriptional or translational machinery.
source: Small molecule metabolites bind mRNA transcripts, usually in the 5′ UTR, to induce a structural change that interferes with the transcriptional or translational machinery (Winkler and Breaker, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work and represents established knowledge about riboswitches.

claim: TPP riboswitches have been identified in plants and fungi.
source: Although most riboswitches have been identified within the bacterial mRNA 5′ UTR, TPP riboswitches, have also been identified in plants and fungi (Kubodera et al., 2003; Sudarsan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The Bacillus subtilis tryptophan RNA-binding attenuation protein (TRAP) is an example of a protein-metabolite-RNA interaction.
source: One example is the Bacillus subtilis tryptophan RNA-binding attenuation protein (TRAP).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Increasing intracellular tryptophan levels induce TRAP multimerization, which enables mRNA recognition and subsequent translational repression of targets.
source: Increasing intracellular tryptophan levels induce TRAP multimerization, which enables mRNA recognition and subsequent translational repression of targets (Gollnick et al., 1990; Antson et al., 1995; Babitzke et al., 1995; Yakhnin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Several metabolic enzymes have been proposed to 'moonlight' as RNA-binding proteins in 'RNA/Enzyme/Metabolite (REM)' networks.
source: Intriguingly, several metabolic enzymes have been proposed to 'moonlight' as RNA-binding proteins in 'RNA/Enzyme/Metabolite (REM)' networks (Ciesla, 2006; Hentze and Preiss, 2010; Castello et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Cytosolic aconitase demonstrates mutually exclusive enzymatic and RNA-binding functionality, depending upon cellular iron levels.
source: A notable example is cytosolic aconitase, which demonstrates mutually exclusive enzymatic and RNA-binding functionality, depending upon cellular iron levels (Hentze and Argos, 1991; Rouault et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: A number of metabolite-sensitive enzymes have demonstrated RNA-binding activity, including GAPDH, glutamate dehydrogenase, thymidylate synthase, and dihydrofolate reductase.
source: A number of metabolite-sensitive enzymes have also demonstrated RNA-binding activity, including GAPDH, glutamate dehydrogenase, thymidylate synthase, and dihydrofolate reductase (Ryazanov, 1985; Chu et al., 1991, 1993; Preiss et al., 1993; Dollenmaier and Weitz, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Metabolite-mediated post-transcriptional regulation is much more prevalent than previously thought.
source: This growing body of research suggests that metabolite-mediated post-transcriptional regulation is much more prevalent than previously thought.
evidence: This is inferred from the growing body of literature on the topic.

claim: MSI1 N-terminal RRM1 acts as a metabolite sensor.
source: Our results show that MSI1 N-terminal RRM1 acts as a metabolite sensor, the first example of such activity observed for the most abundant RNA-binding motif in eukaryotic genomes.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MSI1 RRM1 is the first example of a metabolite sensor among RRM domain proteins.
source: Our results show that MSI1 N-terminal RRM1 acts as a metabolite sensor, the first example of such activity observed for the most abundant RNA-binding motif in eukaryotic genomes.
evidence: This is claimed based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: A survey of RRM structures in the protein data bank reveals several with a surface cavity on the alpha helical face, which may comprise metabolite-binding pockets.
source: A survey of RRM structures in the protein data bank reveals several with a surface cavity on the alpha helical face, which may comprise metabolite-binding pockets.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of RRM proteins in the PDB.

claim: A network of RNA regulatory proteins act as metabolite sensors, possibly replacing the bacterial riboswitch regulation that appears to have been largely lost in eukaryotes.
source: We predict that a network of RNA regulatory proteins act as metabolite sensors, possibly replacing the bacterial riboswitch regulation that appears to have been largely lost in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a prediction/speculation based on the findings of the manuscript.

claim: RNA-binding by the stem cell translation regulator Musashi-1 (MSI1) is allosterically inhibited by 18–22 carbon ω-9 monounsaturated fatty acids.
source: In this study, we show that RNA-binding by the stem cell translation regulator Musashi-1 (MSI1) is allosterically inhibited by 18–22 carbon ω-9 monounsaturated fatty acids.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract and supported by the experimental data.

claim: The fatty acid binds to the N-terminal RNA Recognition Motif (RRM) of MSI1 and induces a conformational change that prevents RNA association.
source: The fatty acid binds to the N-terminal RNA Recognition Motif (RRM) and induces a conformational change that prevents RNA association.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the experimental and computational data.

claim: Musashi proteins are critical for development of the brain, blood, and epithelium.
source: Musashi proteins are critical for development of the brain, blood, and epithelium.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Stearoyl-CoA desaturase-1 is a MSI1 target.
source: We identify stearoyl-CoA desaturase-1 as a MSI1 target, revealing a feedback loop between ω-9 fatty acid biosynthesis and MSI1 activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the experimental data.

claim: There is a feedback loop between ω-9 fatty acid biosynthesis and MSI1 activity.
source: We identify stearoyl-CoA desaturase-1 as a MSI1 target, revealing a feedback loop between ω-9 fatty acid biosynthesis and MSI1 activity.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: Other RRM proteins could act as metabolite sensors to couple gene expression changes to physiological state.
source: We propose that other RRM proteins could act as metabolite sensors to couple gene expression changes to physiological state.
evidence: This is a proposal/speculation based on the findings of the manuscript.
